_about: Intentional, audited divergences from the verbatim v1 content. The reference sections (src/content/sections/*.html), the live calculator subsystem (src/ui/calculators-live.mjs) and the framework-chart node files (src/content/nodes/<income>/<marker>.json) are generated from main:v1/flowchart.html and are held byte-identical to it by gates 9, 10 and 8, so a figure that goes stale there cannot be fixed by editing those files. Targets: 'section:<view>', 'calculators-live', 'node:<income>/<marker>' (a node correction applies to its detailsHtml only). Each entry below is applied by tools/build-v2.mjs on top of the verbatim text at build time; tools/verify-corrections.mjs (gate 13) proves every 'find' still matches the verbatim source exactly 'count' times, so a v1 change or a silent drift fails the build. Tokens in 'replace': {{fig:key}} -> the figure's display string, {{figval:key}} -> its raw number. Hand-typed derived numbers carry the derivation in 'reason'. Every entry names the audit claim it corrects and the primary source read on 'verified'.

corrections.find: For 2026, the phase-out begins at $201,775 single / $403,550 MFJ and completes at $276,775 single / $553,550 MFJ (Rev. Proc. 2025-32)
corrections.replace: For 2026, the phase-out begins at {{fig:qbi_sstb_phasein_start}} and completes at {{fig:qbi_sstb_phasein_complete}} (Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §4.26)
corrections.reason: The verbatim v1 node gave $201,775 / $403,550 and $276,775 / $553,550. Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §4.26 gives threshold $201,750 (all other returns) / $403,500 (MFJ) and phase-in range amount $276,750 / $553,500; $201,775 / $276,775 are the married-filing-separately figures and $403,550 / $553,550 appear nowhere in the table. Re-derived: the upper end is the threshold plus the phase-in range of $75,000 ($150,000 joint) that P.L. 119-21 §70105(a) wrote into §199A(b)(3)(B) and (d)(3): 201,750 + 75,000 = 276,750; 403,500 + 150,000 = 553,500. The rest of the sentence (the $50K/$100K to $75K/$150K expansion) matches §70105(a). Also claim CL360.

corrections.find: OBBBA made the $10K SALT cap permanent (with limited phase-in increases for households under $500K AGI), leaving the PTET election
corrections.replace: OBBBA raised the SALT cap to $40,400 for 2026 (rising 1% a year through 2029, then back to $10,000 from 2030), reduced by 30% of modified AGI above $505,000 but not below $10,000, leaving the PTET election
corrections.reason: The verbatim v1 node said OBBBA made the $10K SALT cap permanent. P.L. 119-21 §70120 (new 26 U.S.C. §164(b)(7)) sets the cap at $40,400 for 2026, 101% of the prior year's amount for 2027-2029 and $10,000 from 2030, reduced by 30% of modified AGI above $505,000 (2026) but not below $10,000 (half amounts for married filing separately, not stated on the page). Every number in the replacement is read from the statute; none is derived. The same paragraph's $400K PTET worked example (approximately $13K recovered) is NOT changed: it rests on unstated assumptions (state tax rate, other SALT paid, filing status, modified AGI), so it is flagged to the owner rather than recomputed. Since 2026-11-23 that example is corrected separately by COR-009 (owner's decision).

P.L. 119-21 §70413(b) struck $10,000 and inserted $20,000 in the last sentence of 26 U.S.C. §529(e)(3) for taxable years beginning after 2025-12-31. Only the figure is changed. Not added (new content, owner's call): §70413(a) also widened the K-12 expenses that count beyond tuition (curriculum, books, online materials, outside tutoring, test fees, dual enrollment, certain therapies) for distributions after enactment.

corrections.find: For a CA business owner in the 37% federal bracket with $400K of pass-through income, PTET recovers approximately $13K of otherwise-capped federal SALT deduction annually.
corrections.replace: For a California owner whose household MAGI is above about $606,000 (where the 2026 cap has phased down to its $10,000 floor) and whose other state and local taxes already use that $10,000, electing California's 9.3% PTET on $400K of pass-through income moves $37,200 of state tax to the entity, where it is federally deductible; at a 35–37% federal rate that saves about $13,000–$13,800 a year. Below $505,000 of MAGI the 2026 cap is $40,400, so up to $40,400 of state and local tax is deductible even without the election, and the saving is smaller unless the owner's other state and local taxes already come close to that cap; how much smaller depends on the owner's other itemized deductions (an owner who would switch to the standard deduction once the election takes the state tax off the personal return gains more than one who itemizes either way).
corrections.reason: The verbatim v1 example (a CA owner in the 37% bracket with $400K of pass-through income 'recovers approximately $13K of ... deduction') was built for a flat $10,000 SALT cap and did not state its assumptions. Under P.L. 119-21 §70120 the 2026 cap is $40,400, reduced by 30% of modified AGI above $505,000 but not below $10,000, so the example holds only once the cap is at its floor. The replacement names that condition and shows the 2026 case below $505,000. Derivation (hand-typed, not figures-layer values): PTET = 9.3% x $400,000 = $37,200 (FTB). The cap reaches its $10,000 floor at MAGI 505,000 + (40,400 - 10,000) / 0.30 = $606,333 ('about $606,000'). At the floor, with other state and local taxes already using the $10,000, the whole $37,200 is an extra federal deduction, whether or not the owner itemizes (the personal SALT deduction is $10,000 either way): 37,200 x 35% = $13,020 and x 37% = $13,764 ('about $13,000-$13,800'; v1's '$13K' was this tax saving, mislabelled as a deduction). 35-37%: a single return above about $606,000 of MAGI is at 35% (over $256,225 but not over $640,600) or 37% (over $640,600); a joint return is at 35% up to $768,700 of taxable income (over $512,450) and 37% above it. A joint return with more than about $94,000 of deductions at that income (606,333 - 512,450) would fall to 32%, a case the stated-rate wording does not cover. Below $505,000 of MAGI no dollar figure is given, because the saving depends on whether the owner itemizes. With $10,000 of other state and local taxes and X of other itemized deductions: without the election the owner itemizes $40,400 + X (more than the 2026 standard deduction of $32,200 joint / $16,100 single, Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §4.14); with it the entity deducts $37,200 and the owner takes the larger of $10,000 + X or the standard deduction. Itemizing either way, the gain is 37,200 + 10,000 - 40,400 = $6,800 of deduction. Switching to the standard deduction (X under $22,200 joint, under $6,100 single), the gain is 37,200 + 32,200 - 40,400 - X = $29,000 - X joint, or 37,200 + 16,100 - 40,400 - X = $12,900 - X single. Below $505,000 of MAGI the rate is at most 32% joint (taxable income under $512,450) or 35% single, so every such gain (at most $9,280 joint, $4,515 single) is below the $13,000 high case; the saving reaches the high case only when other state and local taxes alone approach the $40,400 cap, hence 'unless ... come close to that cap'. Drafts dropped on 2026-11-23: the options report's '$2,200-$2,500' (32-37%; 37% cannot apply below $505,000 of MAGI) and this entry's first '$1,600-$2,400 at 24-35%' (true only for an owner who itemizes both ways; a reviewer found it off by 3-4x for owners who switch to the standard deduction). QBI is not on the page: IRS Notice 2020-75 says the payments are deductible 'in computing its non-separately stated taxable income or loss' but does not mention §199A, and Treas. Reg. §1.199A-3(b)(2)(vi) says only that 'deductions attributable to a trade or business are taken into account for purposes of computing QBI'; no source read states that a PTET payment reduces QBI. Also not modelled, as in v1: the §68 2/37 limit on itemized deductions in the 37% bracket (P.L. 119-21 §70111), married-filing-separately half amounts, head-of-household figures, and California's own rate schedule (the 9.3% PTET is credited against it).
corrections.source: P.L. 119-21 §70120 (26 U.S.C. §164(b)(6)-(7) as amended), https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/119/public/21?link-type=html; California FTB, Pass-through entity (PTE) elective tax, https://www.ftb.ca.gov/file/business/credits/pass-through-entity-elective-tax/index.html ('The PTE elective tax is 9.3% of the qualified entity's qualified net income'); Rev. Proc. 2025-32 §4.01 Tables 1-3 and §4.14, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf; IRS Notice 2020-75, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-20-75.pdf; Treas. Reg. §1.199A-3 (eCFR, as of 2026-11-01)

corrections.find: State election deadlines vary; many require election by March 15 of the prior tax year (i.e., to elect for tax year 2026, the election was typically due March 15, 2025).
corrections.replace: State election deadlines vary. In California the election is made on the entity's timely filed original return for the year (it cannot be made on an amended return), and the required first payment is due by June 15 of that same year; for 2026 through 2030 a missed or short June 15 payment no longer blocks the election, but it cuts the owners' credit by 12.5% of their share of the unpaid amount.
corrections.reason: The verbatim v1 sentence said many states require the election by March 15 of the prior tax year (for 2026, by March 15, 2025). For California, the state the paragraph's example names, that is wrong: the FTB says the annual election is made on a timely filed original return (not an amended return), with the required initial payment due by June 15 of the taxable year of the election, and for taxable years 2026 through 2030 a missed or short June 15 payment no longer prevents the election; the owners' credit is reduced by 12.5% of their pro rata share of the unpaid amount instead. The prior-year March 15 rule is dropped rather than restated for other states, because no other state's rule was read. The paragraph's next sentences ('Check state PTET-statute specifics ...'; 'Missed elections are not curable retroactively') are unchanged; the second agrees with the FTB's 'The election cannot be made on an amended return.'
corrections.source: California FTB, Pass-through entity (PTE) elective tax, https://www.ftb.ca.gov/file/business/credits/pass-through-entity-elective-tax/index.html (page last updated 04/23/2026)

corrections.find: The Social Security trustees project OASI trust fund reserve depletion around 2032–2033 (combined OASI+DI funds in 2034) absent policy intervention — roughly seven to eight years out as of the 2025–2026 reports, not a distant abstraction — with current benefits payable from ongoing payroll taxes at roughly 77–81% of scheduled levels thereafter.
corrections.replace: The Social Security trustees project trust fund reserve depletion absent policy intervention — {{fig:ss_oasi_depletion}} in the latest Trustees Report, well under a decade out, not a distant abstraction — with benefits then payable from ongoing payroll taxes at about {{fig:ss_payable_after_depletion}} of scheduled levels.
corrections.reason: The verbatim v1 sentence gave 'roughly 77–81%' payable (the 2025 report's figures) and 'roughly seven to eight years out as of the 2025–2026 reports'. The 2026 Trustees Report gives OASI depletion in the fourth quarter of 2032 with 78% payable, and combined OASDI in the third quarter of 2034 with 83% payable. Both now come from the figures layer (ss_oasi_depletion, ss_payable_after_depletion), so the expiry gate forces a re-read of the Trustees Report at each refresh instead of leaving hand-typed numbers to drift. 'Well under a decade out' is hand-typed: the fourth quarter of 2032 is about six years from 2026; re-check it at each refresh, and before about 2030. Owner's decision on the 2026-11-16 options report, default C.
corrections.source: SSA, A Summary of the 2026 Annual Reports, https://www.ssa.gov/oact/TRSUM/ (read via Exa web fetch 2026-11-23; a direct request returned HTTP 403)

corrections.find: even at the 77-80% post-depletion benefit level

corrections.reason: Two paragraphs after COR-011, the same §8 repeats the payable share by hand as '77-80%' (the clause CL478 originally tracked).
